Darwin’s Theory of Evolution
¨Each of the 13 species of Galápagos finches has a beak adapted to a particular way of life.
¤A heavy beak is suited to a diet of large seeds
¤The beak of the warbler-finch is suited to feeding on insects
¤A longer, somewhat decurved beak and the split tongue of the cactus-finch are suited to probing a cactus for seeds
explanation: The Galápagos Islands are home to 13 distinct species of finches, each displaying a beak shape adapted to a specific ecological niche and diet. Darwin noted these adaptations: a heavy, robust beak is suited for cracking open large seeds; the warbler-finch possesses a thin beak suited for catching and feeding on insects; and the cactus-finch has a longer, slightly downward-curved (decurved) beak and a split tongue, features adapted for probing cactus flowers and fruits to obtain seeds.

questions.q: How many species of Galápagos finches did Darwin note, and how do their beaks differ?
opts: 5 species; all have heavy beaks for seeds.
13 species; each has a beak adapted to a particular way of life and diet.
13 species; all have long, decurved beaks for nectar.
22 species; they do not show any variation in beak shape.
questions.exp: The notes mention that there are 13 species of Galápagos finches, each with a beak adapted to a particular way of life (such as heavy beaks for large seeds, thin warbler-finch beaks for insects, and long decurved beaks for cactus probing).

questions.q: What diet is the long, decurved beak and split tongue of the cactus-finch adapted for?
questions.exp: The cactus-finch's longer, decurved beak and split tongue are adapted for probing a cactus for seeds.
